Procedure. This article analyzes Swahili compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule. This rule outlines the procedure for constructing a complete word using morphemes. Parentheses in this rule indicate boundaries and are deleted to signify that word formation rules do not access the structure of words formed at previous levels. This study was conducted after it was observed that some Swahili compound nouns violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, especially when changes occur in the middle of the word after various morphemes are combined. The following compound noun illustrates the changes that happen in the middle of a word after various morphemes are joined: [mw [enyekiti]] → [we [enyeviti]]. In this study, we collected data from the Kamusi Kuu ya Kiswahili (2015), where thirty compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule were used as primary data. These nouns were selected based on the distinctive features of violating the Parenthesis Deletion Rule (PDR). This study was guided by one pillar of the Lexical Morphology theory established by Kiparsky (1982) and developed by Katamba and Stonham (2019): the Parenthesis Deletion Rule. The theory of Lexical Morphology emerged to compensate for Chomsky's Generative Grammar perspective, which did not recognize morphology as a distinct level of language. Essentially, this theory demonstrates the relationship between the rules that form morphological structures and the rules that govern how those structures are pronounced. The data related to the research topic was collected from the library. Some of the works used in this study include previous dissertations, online articles, and journals. This research was guided by purposive sampling to identify relevant compound nouns with distinctive features. The findings of this study were presented through charts, tables, and explanations. This research contributes to linguistics, particularly by understanding and explaining compounding strategies in the Swahili language. This is a branch of linguistics that deals with the structure of words (Habwe and Karanja, 2004). Haspelmath and Sims (2013) define morphology as a branch of linguistics that examines the internal structure of words. Based on these definitions, we agree with these scholars' views that morphology is a branch of linguistics concerned with the structure of words. Morphology as a discipline is divided into two main branches: inflectional morphology and word formation morphology. Inflectional morphology deals with the process of inflection in words, where inflectional affixes are added to word roots to represent various meanings, but these inflections do not change the word class. Word formation morphology is the field that addresses the linguistic processes and outcomes of creating new words by adding affixes to word roots, where a derivational affix forms a new word (Mgullu, 1999; Katamba & Stonham, 2019). Word formation in Swahili takes place through various methods. These methods follow a specific procedure for generating forms with different characteristics. These methods include borrowing, abbreviation (acronyms, blending, and clipping), and extension.  
The compounding method uses complete words formed through various processes as raw material to create entirely new words. The resulting forms are written by joining two words together, using hyphens, or leaving a space between the combined words (Gichuru, 2010). However, in this article we decided to write these compound nouns in two ways; that is, by combining all the words and by separating some of the words in these compound nouns in order to simplify the analysis of the data conducted. Mgullu (1999) views compound nouns as complex morphemes. He states that complex morphemes are morphemes formed by joining together at least two stems or roots of words, which, in other contexts, these stems can be separated and each one can be a complete word. Mgullu’s views (already mentioned) are in agreement with those of Mustafa (2020), who maintains that compound nouns are nouns formed by joining two words (roots, stems, free morphemes, or lexical affixes). These two words may be joined with a space, without a space, or with a hyphen. For example, as evident in the compound nouns 'mwanamke' and 'mwalimu mkuu.' The Parenthesis Deletion Rule is a principle used to show the process of constructing a complete word using its morphemes. Parentheses in this rule indicate the boundaries of the various morphemes and are deleted to show that the word formation rules have no access to the structure of words formed at earlier levels (Katamba & Stonham, 2019). The Parenthesis Deletion Rule has an approach that emphasizes that inner parentheses are deleted first at the lexical level. As a result of this approach, words formed in the middle of the lexical level cannot be affected by cyclic phonological rules (Kiparsky, 1982; Katamba and Stonham, 2019). A compound word like the one above, when formed and reaches stage 3, consists of only two morphemes, namely {mw} + {anamke}, unlike in stage 1 where it had the morpheme {{mw}kia. {ana}root + {{m}tail.{ke}root}. According to the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, at stage 3 you cannot separate {ana} and {mke}, and therefore no further changes should occur in this morpheme. In the plural, the compound noun "mwanawake" becomes "wanawake," whereas we know that in the singular there are two morphemes, {mw} and {anamke}. This change within the morpheme {anamke} after the various morphemes have been combined is surprising, since the Parenthesis Deletion Rule does not permit changes to occur within the word after the various morphemes have been joined. Some Swahili compound nouns violate this procedure, and this is the issue being investigated. After deleting the parentheses, words formed through morphology and word formation rules do not allow access to the internal structure of the words. This approach allows for external but not internal reference to a word after the parentheses have been deleted. The first morpheme in the entire word can be placed in the plural form without affecting the second morpheme in the entire word (Allen, 1978; Siegel, 1974). The first morpheme referred to here is the noun class prefix found in the first word of the compound noun, while the second morpheme is that part of the compound noun which carries the root or stem of the first word together with the second or third word in the compound, for example, the compound noun 'mwanamke' consists of two morphemes: {mw} as the first morpheme and {anamke} as the second. Previous Studies  
Katikiro (2018) conducted research on the evaluation of meaning in Swahili compound words. In that study, he addressed the identification of the contribution of the meanings of constituent morphemes to the resultant meaning of the compound word. Referring to Gordian (2010), he asserted that compound words are formed through a morphological process of joining together two words that are different in meaning and form to create a new word with a single meaning or one that refers to a single entity or concept. In this study, Katikiro (2018) focused on the examination of the branch of semantics, which deals with meaning in different constructions, in contrast to the study we conducted, which was concerned with the branch of linguistics known as morphology. However, the knowledge gained from this study was useful to us in understanding the morphological process of forming compound nouns by joining together two words that are different in meaning and form to create a single concept. Extensive reading of articles in the library, books, and online articles was intended to obtain important information about the violation of the Parenthesis Deletion Rule of Lexical Morphology in the formation of Swahili compound nouns and also to understand the compounding method in the Swahili language. The information obtained was instrumental in identifying the gap addressed by this study. Gituru (2019), in his study on verb inflection in Kigĩchũgũ, identified the processes and sequences of Kigĩchũgũ verbs during inflection, guided by the theory of Lexical Morphology and the Mirror Principle. Additionally, in this investigation, he demonstrated that the Parenthesis Deletion Rule illustrates the changes that verbs undergo during inflection, with various forms combining into a single verb. This study formed the basis for explaining the procedure of the Parenthesis Deletion Rule in the word formation process and provided further explanations about the theory of Lexical Morphology. Buberwa (2017), in examining the morphological patterns of place names in the Haya language, identified the arrangement of morphemes that form these names and demonstrated how the morphemes are linearly ordered, guided by the principle of the Lexical Level Rule of Lexical Morphology. In that study, he explained the theory of Lexical Morphology clearly. However, the main difference between Buberwa’s (2017) research and this study is that his research examined the arrangement of words in the Haya language and demonstrated how morphemes are sequenced, guided by the principle of the Lexical Level Rule of Lexical Morphology. On the other hand, the study we conducted examined Swahili compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule of Lexical Morphology. This study was useful to us in explaining the concept of Lexical Morphology theory. Odden (2019), in his study on tone prediction in Kikuria, identified that the Parenthesis Deletion Rule is violated in the placement of tone in Kikuria verbs, especially the rule of stem shift when the stem’s internal parentheses are exposed. He goes on to say that this situation occurs when the tone is shifted from the prefix to the stem of the Kikuria verb, thereby violating the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, which does not allow phonology to refer to the internal morphology of the word. The knowledge gained from this study was useful in understanding the entire process of compound noun formation and how some of these nouns violate the rule. Buberwa (2011), in his research on the structure of place names, identified noun formation strategies such as semantic shift, toponyms, eponyms, and the compounding method, which are used in creating names for bus stops in the city of Dar es Salaam. This study was similar to ours in that it addressed the method of compounding; however, it differs because our study examined Swahili compound nouns. His study drew its data from Nyuso za Mwanamke (2010), Kamusi ya Isimu na Falsafa ya Lugha (2004), and Kamusi ya Kiswahili Sanifu (2004). In his research on eliminating cyclicity as a source of phonological difficulty, Cole (1995) identified the internal morphology of the word as being accessible to phonology even after the word has been fully formed. He goes on to state that the internal morphological structure of the word must be visible in order to capture the effects of cyclicity by imposing constraints within domains that are morphologically defined. From this analysis, we gained insight into how internal morphology is reflected in phonology, a situation that contrasts with the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, which allows phonology to refer only to the external structure of the word. This helped us to recognize how some Swahili compound nouns violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule by permitting phonology to access the internal structure of the compound noun after various morphemes have been joined. However, these studies differ in that Gichuru (2010) focused on analyzing the formation of Swahili compound nouns and their grammatical inflection, guided by the six principles of Lexical Morphology (the Strict Cycle Principle, the Lexical Level Principle, the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, the Structure Preservation Principle, the Feature Minimality Principle, and the Elsewhere Condition of Lexical Morphology), whereas this study was concerned with examining compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule by taking plural morphemes for all the words that form the respective compound noun. The knowledge about compound nouns and the theory of Lexical Morphology from this study was useful in the research of this particular topic. This review of the literature has revealed that although there are studies that have been conducted regarding the compounding method of forming Swahili nouns, the violation of the Parenthesis Deletion Rule has not been clearly articulated. Therefore, this article highlights some Swahili compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, especially when they accept changes occurring in the middle of the word after the various morphemes have been joined. Swahili Compound Nouns That Violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule

This article addresses Swahili compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule by allowing changes to occur in the middle of the word after the various morphemes have been combined. These changes take place when the second morpheme in the compound noun takes plural affixes, which is contrary to the Parenthesis Deletion Rule that only allows phonology to reference the outermost boundaries established during the morphological formation of the word. After removing the parentheses, the words formed by combining morphological segments are treated as if they have never been combined; thus, they are considered whole from the beginning. The Optimal Shape Theory holds that all morphological information is visible to phonology (Prince and Smolensky, 1993). This view aligns with that of Cole (1995), who argues that the internal structure of a word’s morphology must be visible in order to obtain cyclic effects by imposing restrictions within morphologically defined domains. In this study, we have demonstrated some Swahili compound nouns that violate the Bracket Erasure Rule by allowing changes to occur in the second morpheme of the compound noun that we listed in Table 2, where they take plural markers. Maana ya maneno, majina ya mahali, majina ya watu, na maneno yanayounganishwa (Rubanza, 1996; Buberwa, 2011; Matinde, 2012). Mada ya makala hii ipo ndani ya eneo la jumla la mofolojia. Hii ni tawi la isimu linaloshughulikia muundo wa maneno (Habwe na Karanja, 2004). Haspelmath na Sims (2013) wanafafanua mofolojia kama tawi la isimu linalochunguza muundo wa ndani wa maneno. Kulingana na tafsiri hizi, tunakubaliana na maoni ya wasomi hawa kwamba mofolojia ni tawi la isimu linalohusika na muundo wa maneno. Mofolojia kama taaluma imegawanywa katika matawi mawili makuu: mofolojia ya uambishaji na mofolojia ya utengenezaji maneno. Mofolojia ya uambishaji hushughulika na mchakato wa uambishaji katika maneno, ambapo vihirizi vya uambishaji vinaongezwa kwenye mizizi ya maneno ili kuwakilisha maana mbalimbali, lakini mabadiliko haya hayabadilishi aina ya neno. Mofolojia ya utengenezaji maneno ni eneo linaloshughulikia michakato ya kiisimu na matokeo ya kuunda maneno mapya kwa kuongeza vihirizi kwenye mizizi ya maneno, ambapo kihirizi kinazalisha neno jipya (Mgullu, 1999; Katamba & Stonham, 2019). Utengenezaji wa maneno katika Kiswahili hufanyika kupitia mbinu mbalimbali. Mbinu hizi hufuata utaratibu maalum wa kuzalisha maneno yenye tabia tofauti. Mbinu hizi ni pamoja na uazimaji, ufupishaji (vifupisho, kuchanganya na kukata), na upanuzi. Mbinu ya muunganiko hutumia maneno kamili yaliyoundwa kupitia michakato mbalimbali kama malighafi ya kuunda maneno mapya kabisa. Maneno yanayopatikana huandikwa kwa kuunganisha maneno mawili pamoja, kutumia vistari, au kuacha nafasi kati ya maneno yaliyounganishwa (Gichuru, 2010). Hata hivyo, katika makala hii tumeamua kuandika nomino changamano kwa njia mbili; yaani, kwa kuunganisha maneno yote na kwa kutenganisha baadhi ya maneno katika nomino hizi changamano ili kurahisisha uchambuzi wa data uliofanywa. Mgullu (1999) anaona nomino changamano kama mofimu changamano. Anaeleza kuwa mofimu changamano ni mofimu zinazoundwa kwa kuunganisha angalau mizizi miwili ya maneno, ambayo, katika muktadha mwingine, mizizi hii inaweza kutenganishwa na kila moja kuwa neno kamili. Maoni ya Mgullu (tayari yametajwa) yanakubaliana na yale ya Mustafa (2020), ambaye anasisitiza kwamba nomino tatanishi ni nomino zinazoundwa kwa kuunganisha maneno mawili (mizizi, vijisekta, mofimu huru, au viambajengo leksikali). Maneno haya mawili yanaweza kuunganishwa kwa nafasi, bila nafasi, au kwa kutumia alama ya kistari. Kwa mfano, kama inavyoonekana katika nomino ambatani 'mwanamke' na 'mwalimu mkuu.' Kanuni hii inashikilia kwamba baada ya mabano ya ndani kuondolewa, sheria za utengenezaji maneno hazina ufikiaji wa muundo wa ndani wa maneno. Lengo kuu la makala hii ni kuonyesha majina ambatano ya Kiswahili yanayokiuka Kanuni ya Kufuta Mabano kama inavyoelekezwa na nguzo moja; Kanuni ya Kufuta Mabano ya Mofolojia ya Leksika (Kiparsky, 1982). Makala haya yanazungumzia nomino tamili za Kiswahili zinazokiuka Kanuni ya Kufuta Parenthesis kwa kuruhusu mabadiliko kutokea katikati ya neno baada ya mofimu mbalimbali kuunganishwa. Mabadiliko haya hutokea wakati mofimu ya pili katika nomino tamili inapochukua viambishi vya wingi, kinyume cha Kanuni ya Kufuta Parenthesis ambayo inaruhusu fonolojia kurejelea mipaka ya nje pekee iliyoanzishwa wakati wa uundaji wa neno kimofolojia. Katika utafiti wa maktaba tulioufanya, tulibaini nomino tamili thelathini zinazokiuka Kanuni ya Kufuta Parenthesis, ambazo zimeorodheshwa kwenye Jedwali la 2. Data ya nomino ambatano zilizoorodheshwa kwenye Jedwali la 2 inaonyesha ukiukwaji wa Kanuni ya Kuondoa Mabano. Kanuni hii inatumia mbinu inayosisitiza kwamba mabano ya ndani yanaondolewa kwanza katika ngazi ya msamiati, na ikiwa kuna marejeleo katika nomino tata, marejeleo hayo ni kwa mofimu ya kwanza tu (Allen, 1978; Kiparsky, 1982; Katamba na Stonham, 2019). Ili kutoa mwanga zaidi kuhusu ukiukaji wa Kanuni ya Kuondoa Mabano, tutaelezea mchakato wa kutengeneza nomino ambatano ‘mjamzito’ kutoka Jedwali la 2 kama mwakilishi wa nomino nyingine 29 zilizoainishwa hapo juu, kama inavyoonyeshwa kwenye Mchoro 1 hapa chini:

Hata hivyo, Orgun na Inkelas (2002) wanadai kuibuka kwa nadharia inayofichua mofolojia ya ndani kwa fonolojia hata baada ya neno kukamilika kabisa, yaani nadharia ya Umbo la Prosodi. Kuondolewa huku kwa uandishi marudufu wa asili kutoka kwa neno la kwanza kunaonekana wazi katika nomino changamano tulizoorodhesha kwenye Jedwali la 3. Odden (2019) anadai kwamba Kanuni ya Kufutwa kwa Mabano inakiukwa katika ugawaji wa toni kwenye vitenzi vya Kikuria, hasa kwenye sheria ya uondoaji wa mzizi inapokutana na mabano ya ndani ndani ya mzizi, kama inavyoonekana katika vitenzi tuùre na gi–tùùre kuashiria 'nimechukua hicho.' Hali hii hutokea pale toni inapofutwa kutoka kwa kiambishi na kuhamishiwa kwenye mzizi wa kitenzi cha Kikuria, hivyo kukiuka Kanuni ya Kufutwa kwa Mabano, ambayo hairuhusu fonolojia kurejelea mofolojia ya ndani ya neno. Kinachotokea katika Mfano wa 3 ni kwamba, katika nomino ambatano ‘mkazamjomba,’ katika mzunguko wa kwanza, shadda inatolewa kwa nomino ‘mkaza’ na ‘mjomba’, yaani, [[mꞌkaza]] [[mꞌjomba]]. Katika mzunguko wa pili, mabano ya ndani yanafutwa; kulingana na kanuni ya mzunguko, kuondolewa kwa msisitizo mkuu kutoka kwa nomino 'mkaza' na ugawaji upya wa msisitizo mkuu kwenye nomino 'mjomba' kunafanya msisitizo mkuu katika nomino 'mkaza' kuwa dhaifu, hivyo msisitizo mkuu unaondolewa na kuwekwa upya kwenye silabi ya pili kutoka mwisho ya nomino 'mjomba', na kusababisha ‘mkazamꞌjomba.’ Chomsky na Halle (1968) wanadai kuwa msisitizo mkuu unapowekwa katika nafasi fulani kwenye neno, misisitizo mingine katika neno hilo hilo inakuwa dhaifu, kama inavyoonekana katika nomino ambatano ‘mkazamjomba.’ Kuondolewa kwa msisitizo kutoka kwa neno la kwanza na ugawaji wake upya kwenye neno la pili katika mchakato wa Fonolojia ya Mzunguko kunaonyesha kwamba hakuna uvunjaji wa CCC (Sharti la Muundo wa Kiambajengo), kwa sababu kanuni inachukulia hili kama neno moja, si maneno mawili kama awali. Kuondolewa kwa mkazo mkuu katika neno la kwanza hakufanyiki tu katika nomino tetezi za Kiswahili bali pia katika lugha nyingine kama Kihispania. Massamba (2011) anarejelea aina hii ya mkazo, ambao huondolewa kutoka neno la kwanza na kuwekwa kwenye neno la pili, kama mkazo mkuu, na anaendelea kueleza kwamba neno la kwanza, kwa kiasi fulani, katika nomino tetezi, hubakiza mkazo fulani, lakini mkazo huo hauwi tena mkuu; unaweza kuwa wa pili au wa tatu kutegemea maneno yanayounda nomino tetezi husika. Halle, Harris, na Vergnaud (1991) wanaeleza jinsi mkazo unavyotolewa katika nomino tambalanishi za Kihispania, wakiongozwa na mtazamo wa kuondoa mkazo, hasa wakati nomino tambalanishi zinapoondoa mkazo mkuu kutoka kwenye kipengele cha kulia cha tambalanishi na kuurejesha upande wa kushoto wa kipengele husika cha tambalanishi. Kwa mfano, kama inavyoonekana katika nomino tambatamba ya Kihispania ꞌagwaniꞌeve, Orgun na Inkelas (2002) pia walielezea kuwepo kwa changamoto katika matumizi ya Kanuni ya Kufuta Mabano kwenye uundaji wa vitenzi vya Kiingereza, ambapo waligundua kuwa baadhi ya vitenzi vina viambishi vinavyoonekana upande wa nje. Orgun na Inkelas (2002) wanasema zaidi kwamba kilatini cha muundo kinaruhusu uwepo wa kimsingi kingine maalum, yaani, aina hizi za vitenzi. discourses.source_txt: This article analyzes Swahili compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule. This rule outlines the procedure for constructing a complete word using morphemes. Parentheses in this rule indicate boundaries and are deleted to signify that word formation rules do not access the structure of words formed at previous levels.
discourses.translated_txt: Makala haya yanachambua nomino changamano za Kiswahili zinazokiuka Kanuni ya Kufuta Vibano. Kanuni hii inaelezea utaratibu wa kuunda neno kamili kwa kutumia mofimu. Vibano katika kanuni hii vinaonyesha mipaka na hufutwa ili kuashiria kwamba kanuni za uundaji wa maneno haziingilii muundo wa maneno yaliyoundwa katika ngazi za awali.

discourses.source_txt: This study was conducted after it was observed that some Swahili compound nouns violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, especially when changes occur in the middle of the word after various morphemes are combined. The following compound noun illustrates the changes that happen in the middle of a word after various morphemes are joined: [mw [enyekiti]] → [we [enyeviti]]. In this study, we collected data from the Kamusi Kuu ya Kiswahili (2015), where thirty compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule were used as primary data.
discourses.translated_txt: Utafiti huu ulifanyika baada ya kubainika kuwa baadhi ya nomino ambatano za Kiswahili zinakiuka Kanuni ya Ufutaji wa Vifungo, hasa pale mabadiliko yanapotokea katikati ya neno baada ya mofimu mbalimbali kuunganishwa. Nomino ambatano ifuatayo inaonyesha mabadiliko yanayotokea katikati ya neno baada ya mofimu mbalimbali kuunganishwa: [mw [enyekiti]] → [we [enyeviti]]. Katika utafiti huu, tulikusanya data kutoka katika Kamusi Kuu ya Kiswahili (2015), ambapo nomino ambatano thelathini zinazokiuka Kanuni ya Ufutaji wa Vifungo zilitumika kama data msingi.

discourses.source_txt: This study was guided by one pillar of the Lexical Morphology theory established by Kiparsky (1982) and developed by Katamba and Stonham (2019): the Parenthesis Deletion Rule.

discourses.source_txt: The theory of Lexical Morphology emerged to compensate for Chomsky's Generative Grammar perspective, which did not recognize morphology as a distinct level of language. Essentially, this theory demonstrates the relationship between the rules that form morphological structures and the rules that govern how those structures are pronounced.

discourses.source_txt: The data related to the research topic was collected from the library. Some of the works used in this study include previous dissertations, online articles, and journals. This research was guided by purposive sampling to identify relevant compound nouns with distinctive features. The findings of this study were presented through charts, tables, and explanations. This research contributes to linguistics, particularly by understanding and explaining compounding strategies in the Swahili language.

discourses.source_txt: The topic of this article falls within the general area of morphology. This is a branch of linguistics that deals with the structure of words (Habwe and Karanja, 2004). Haspelmath and Sims (2013) define morphology as a branch of linguistics that examines the internal structure of words. Based on these definitions, we agree with these scholars' views that morphology is a branch of linguistics concerned with the structure of words.
discourses.translated_txt: Mada ya makala hii ipo ndani ya eneo la jumla la mofolojia. Hii ni tawi la isimu linaloshughulikia muundo wa maneno (Habwe na Karanja, 2004). Haspelmath na Sims (2013) wanafafanua mofolojia kama tawi la isimu linalochunguza muundo wa ndani wa maneno. Kulingana na tafsiri hizi, tunakubaliana na maoni ya wasomi hawa kwamba mofolojia ni tawi la isimu linalohusika na muundo wa maneno.

discourses.source_txt: Morphology as a discipline is divided into two main branches: inflectional morphology and word formation morphology. Inflectional morphology deals with the process of inflection in words, where inflectional affixes are added to word roots to represent various meanings, but these inflections do not change the word class. Word formation morphology is the field that addresses the linguistic processes and outcomes of creating new words by adding affixes to word roots, where a derivational affix forms a new word (Mgullu, 1999; Katamba & Stonham, 2019). Word formation in Swahili takes place through various methods.
discourses.translated_txt: Mofolojia kama taaluma imegawanywa katika matawi mawili makuu: mofolojia ya uambishaji na mofolojia ya utengenezaji maneno. Mofolojia ya uambishaji hushughulika na mchakato wa uambishaji katika maneno, ambapo vihirizi vya uambishaji vinaongezwa kwenye mizizi ya maneno ili kuwakilisha maana mbalimbali, lakini mabadiliko haya hayabadilishi aina ya neno. Mofolojia ya utengenezaji maneno ni eneo linaloshughulikia michakato ya kiisimu na matokeo ya kuunda maneno mapya kwa kuongeza vihirizi kwenye mizizi ya maneno, ambapo kihirizi kinazalisha neno jipya (Mgullu, 1999; Katamba & Stonham, 2019). Utengenezaji wa maneno katika Kiswahili hufanyika kupitia mbinu mbalimbali.

discourses.source_txt:
These methods follow a specific procedure for generating forms with different characteristics. These methods include borrowing, abbreviation (acronyms, blending, and clipping), and extension.  
The compounding method uses complete words formed through various processes as raw material to create entirely new words. The resulting forms are written by joining two words together, using hyphens, or leaving a space between the combined words (Gichuru, 2010).
discourses.translated_txt: Mbinu hizi hufuata utaratibu maalum wa kuzalisha maneno yenye tabia tofauti. Mbinu hizi ni pamoja na uazimaji, ufupishaji (vifupisho, kuchanganya na kukata), na upanuzi. Mbinu ya muunganiko hutumia maneno kamili yaliyoundwa kupitia michakato mbalimbali kama malighafi ya kuunda maneno mapya kabisa. Maneno yanayopatikana huandikwa kwa kuunganisha maneno mawili pamoja, kutumia vistari, au kuacha nafasi kati ya maneno yaliyounganishwa (Gichuru, 2010).

discourses.source_txt: However, in this article we decided to write these compound nouns in two ways; that is, by combining all the words and by separating some of the words in these compound nouns in order to simplify the analysis of the data conducted. Mgullu (1999) views compound nouns as complex morphemes. He states that complex morphemes are morphemes formed by joining together at least two stems or roots of words, which, in other contexts, these stems can be separated and each one can be a complete word.
discourses.translated_txt: Hata hivyo, katika makala hii tumeamua kuandika nomino changamano kwa njia mbili; yaani, kwa kuunganisha maneno yote na kwa kutenganisha baadhi ya maneno katika nomino hizi changamano ili kurahisisha uchambuzi wa data uliofanywa. Mgullu (1999) anaona nomino changamano kama mofimu changamano. Anaeleza kuwa mofimu changamano ni mofimu zinazoundwa kwa kuunganisha angalau mizizi miwili ya maneno, ambayo, katika muktadha mwingine, mizizi hii inaweza kutenganishwa na kila moja kuwa neno kamili.

discourses.source_txt: Mgullu’s views (already mentioned) are in agreement with those of Mustafa (2020), who maintains that compound nouns are nouns formed by joining two words (roots, stems, free morphemes, or lexical affixes). These two words may be joined with a space, without a space, or with a hyphen.
discourses.translated_txt: Maoni ya Mgullu (tayari yametajwa) yanakubaliana na yale ya Mustafa (2020), ambaye anasisitiza kwamba nomino tatanishi ni nomino zinazoundwa kwa kuunganisha maneno mawili (mizizi, vijisekta, mofimu huru, au viambajengo leksikali). Maneno haya mawili yanaweza kuunganishwa kwa nafasi, bila nafasi, au kwa kutumia alama ya kistari.

discourses.source_txt: In his research on eliminating cyclicity as a source of phonological difficulty, Cole (1995) identified the internal morphology of the word as being accessible to phonology even after the word has been fully formed. He goes on to state that the internal morphological structure of the word must be visible in order to capture the effects of cyclicity by imposing constraints within domains that are morphologically defined. From this analysis, we gained insight into how internal morphology is reflected in phonology, a situation that contrasts with the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, which allows phonology to refer only to the external structure of the word. This helped us to recognize how some Swahili compound nouns violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule by permitting phonology to access the internal structure of the compound noun after various morphemes have been joined.
discourses.translated_txt: Katika utafiti wake juu ya kuondoa mzunguko kama chanzo cha ugumu wa kifonolojia, Cole (1995) alitambua mofolojia ya ndani ya neno kuwa inapatikana kwa fonolojia hata baada ya neno kuundwa kikamilifu. Kutokana na uchambuzi huu, tulipata uelewa wa jinsi mofolojia ya ndani inavyojitokeza katika fonolojia, hali ambayo ni tofauti na Kanuni ya Kufuta Parenthesis, ambayo inairuhusu fonolojia kurejelea tu muundo wa nje wa neno. Swahili Compound Nouns That Violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule

This article addresses Swahili compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule by allowing changes to occur in the middle of the word after the various morphemes have been combined. These changes take place when the second morpheme in the compound noun takes plural affixes, which is contrary to the Parenthesis Deletion Rule that only allows phonology to reference the outermost boundaries established during the morphological formation of the word. In the library-based study we conducted, we identified thirty compound nouns that violate the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, which are listed in Table 2.

Mabadiliko haya hutokea wakati mofimu ya pili katika nomino tamili inapochukua viambishi vya wingi, kinyume cha Kanuni ya Kufuta Parenthesis ambayo inaruhusu fonolojia kurejelea mipaka ya nje pekee iliyoanzishwa wakati wa uundaji wa neno kimofolojia. Katika utafiti wa maktaba tulioufanya, tulibaini nomino tamili thelathini zinazokiuka Kanuni ya Kufuta Parenthesis, ambazo zimeorodheshwa kwenye Jedwali la 2.

The plural marker should be placed on the first morpheme, that is, {m}, and not on the second morpheme {jamzito}. According to the Parenthesis Deletion Rule, the grammatical inflection of the compound noun in the plural should be ٭wajamzito, a noun that creates grammatical ambiguity. The Optimal Shape Theory holds that all morphological information is visible to phonology (Prince and Smolensky, 1993). This view aligns with that of Cole (1995), who argues that the internal structure of a word’s morphology must be visible in order to obtain cyclic effects by imposing restrictions within morphologically defined domains. The perspectives of Orgun and Inkelas (2002) and Cole (1995) differ from those of scholars such as Siegel (1974), Allen (1978), Pesetsky (1979), Kiparsky (1982), Mohanan (1986), Inkelas (1990), Booij (1997), and Katamba & Stonham (2019), who maintain that after parentheses are deleted in the process of word formation, the Bracket Erasure Rule allows phonology to refer to only the outermost boundaries set in morphological structure, but does not permit reference to internal forms. In this study, we have demonstrated some Swahili compound nouns that violate the Bracket Erasure Rule by allowing changes to occur in the second morpheme of the compound noun that we listed in Table 2, where they take plural markers. For example: in the compound noun morphemes ‘mkemwenza,’ the first morpheme [m] and the second morpheme [kemwenza] take the plural form as [wa[kewenza]]. According to Orgun and Inkelas (2002), when parentheses are deleted in the process of forming this compound noun, the Bracket Erasure Rule does not allow phonology to refer to internal forms, for instance, the second morpheme {jamzito}. Nouns formed from verbs indicate the boundary of compounding in their context. What Orgun and Inkelas (2002) and Poser (1990) mean is the case of the loss of gemination in Japanese nouns formed from verbs. Insights from the violation of the Bracket Erasure Rule in Japanese nouns formed from verbs helped us understand the entire phonological process regarding the internal structures of the word and how these compound nouns undergo regemination. The following Table 3 illustrates the manner in which gemination is reapplied in Swahili compound nouns, as is evident in the Japanese language where phonology appears to require greater access to the internal structure of the word than what the Bracket Erasure Rule allows in referencing external boundaries established in morphological derivation. discourses.source_txt: In the second cycle, the inner brackets are deleted; according to the cycle rule, the removal of the primary stress from the noun ‘mkaza’ and the reassignment of the primary stress onto the noun ‘mjomba’ renders the primary stress in the noun ‘mkaza’ weak, thus the primary stress is removed and newly placed on the penultimate syllable of the noun ‘mjomba,’ resulting in ‘mkazamꞌjomba.’ Chomsky and Halle (1968) claim that when primary stress is assigned to a particular position in a word, other stresses in the same word become weak, as is evident in the compound noun ‘mkazamjomba.’ The removal of stress from the first word and its reassignment on the second word in the process of Cyclic Phonology demonstrates that there is no violation of the CCC (Constituent Structure Constraint), because the rule considers this as a single word, not two words as before.

discourses.source_txt: Morphological patterns require that the internal structure of the stem be visible to the external morpheme. This situation, where the internal structure is apparent to the external morpheme, is observed in compound nouns in Swahili that violate the Bracketing Erasure Principle, particularly when the second morphemes take plural markers. For instance, we shall use the compound noun 'mwanamke' as a representative of the nouns listed in Table 3 to show how the internal structure becomes visible to the external morpheme. The compound noun 'mwanamke' consists of two morphemes: {mw} and {anamke}, and when this compound noun is grammatically pluralized, the first morpheme {mw} and the second morpheme {anamke} both take plural prefixes to become {w} and {anawake}. This situation demonstrates how the prefix {m} of the noun ‘mke’ in the second morpheme {anamke} becomes visible to the first morpheme {mw}, and this is the reason why the compound nouns in Table 3 violate the Bracketing Erasure Principle. Conclusion Names of Places in Haya: A Lexical Morphology Perspective.

discourses.source_txt: This article has addressed Swahili compound nouns that violate the Bracket Deletion Principle. In order to demonstrate the existence of Swahili compound nouns which contravene this principle, we were guided by the framework of the Bracket Deletion Principle to explain the process involved in the formation of compound nouns and the ways in which these compounds violate this process, especially when they are grammatically pluralized, a situation that leads to changes in the middle of the word after various morphemes are joined and the brackets are removed. In summary, this article has explained how some Swahili compound nouns violate the Bracket Deletion Principle by following the pattern [plural + Y1] + [plural + Yn], for example: mkazamwana → wakazawana, which is contrary to the principle since the rule does not allow this type of backward reference after the deletion of brackets. If backward reference does occur, it follows the pattern [plural + Y1] + [Yn], as is evident in the compound noun; mwanamgambo → wanamgambo. Lastly, we observed the removal of the basic gemination from the first part of the compound noun and the reapplication of the basic gemination on the penultimate syllable of the relevant compound noun.
discourses.translated_txt: Makala haya yamezungumzia nomino ambatano za Kiswahili ambazo zinakiuka Kanuni ya Uondoaji Mabanio. Ili kuonyesha uwepo wa nomino ambatano za Kiswahili zinazokiuka kanuni hii, tuliongozwa na mfumo wa Kanuni ya Uondoaji Mabanio kuelezea mchakato unaohusika katika uundaji wa nomino ambatano na namna ambavyo nomino hizi zinakiuka mchakato huu, hasa zinapofanywa wingi kimofolojia, hali inayosababisha mabadiliko katikati ya neno baada ya mofimu mbalimbali kuunganishwa na mabanio kuondolewa. Kwa muhtasari, makala hii imeeleza namna baadhi ya nomino ambatano za Kiswahili zinavyokiuka Kanuni ya Uondoaji Mabanio kwa kufuata mtindo wa [wingi + Y1] + [wingi + Yn], kwa mfano: mkazamwana → wakazawana, jambo ambalo ni kinyume na kanuni kwa kuwa sheria hairuhusu aina hii ya marejeleo ya nyuma baada ya uondoaji wa mabanio. Ikiwa marejeleo ya nyuma yatatokea, hufuata mtindo wa [wingi + Y1] + [Yn], kama inavyoonekana kwenye nomino ambatano; mwanamgambo → wanamgambo. Mwisho, tulitambua kuondolewa kwa ugeminue msingi kutoka sehemu ya kwanza ya nomino ambatano na kurejeshwa kwa ugeminue msingi kwenye silabi ya pili kutoka mwisho ya nomino ambatano husika.
